prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map clearly captures the 3D layout of the doorway scene, showing the right doorframe wall very close to the camera wearer (brightest white, ~0.3–0.5 m), the dog and the wearer's hands in the lower-left foreground (~0.4–1.2 m), the doorway partition wall behind the dog (~1.5 m), and the recessed storage area and left hallway receding into darkness (2–3+ m). Within the foreground, the brightness gradient distinguishes the wearer's left hand (~0.4–0.5 m, holding the dog's neck) and right hand (reaching toward the snout at ~0.5 m in frames 3–5) from the dog's closer head (~0.5–0.7 m, facing forward-right and tilting slightly up in frame 3) and farther hindquarters (~1.0–1.2 m to the left). Compared to the dark fur in the RGB frames, the depth map makes the spatial separation between the dog's head and rear torso—as well as the continuous surface of the floor and walls—immediately legible. However, the map is unreliable inside the dark closet and left hallway where furniture and storage bags (~2–3 m away) flatten into uniform black, and it merges the wearer's touching hands smoothly into the dog's neck and snout contours without sharp depth boundaries.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map isolates the foreground silhouette in the lower-left (roughly 0.4–1.2 m from the camera wearer and within arm's reach) against an unsegmented black background, capturing the combined outline of the dog standing left-to-right and the camera wearer's hands entering from the bottom edge. Across the five frames, the segmented foreground region reflects the dog lifting its head slightly in frame 3 and turning its snout toward the wearer's right hand at the bottom-center in frames 4–5, while the dog's rear remains to the left. While the masks help separate the dark-furred dog from the shadowy floor and doorway corner in frames 1, 2, 4, and 5, the map is highly unreliable in both class labeling and boundary separation. It misclassifies the dog and attached hands as a 'person' in frame 1, an overlapping 'cat'/'dog' in frame 2, and a 'person' again in frame 3 where it completely clips off the dog's hindquarters on the left and falsely segments a vertical laundry bag in the background closet (~2 m away) as another 'person'. Furthermore, in frames 1–3 the wearer's hands are fused into the animal mask, in frame 4 the hands are missed entirely, and in frame 5 the hands and lower chest are split into fragmented purple masks below the green 'dog' mask while all walls, doorframes, and background objects remain unsegmented.
descriptions.pose: The pose map attempts to place yellow body keypoints in the lower-left foreground (~0.5–1.2 m away), where the dog stands within arm's reach and the camera wearer's hands reach in from the bottom of the frame. Because no full human body is visible in the scene—only the camera wearer's two hands at ~0.4–0.5 m and the dog facing right with its head turned toward the wearer's hands—the map provides no reliable skeletal structure and instead produces false-positive human torso/limb skeletons on the dog's body in frames 1–3 and complete blank frames in frames 4–5. Specifically, in frames 1 and 2, yellow body lines falsely span the dog's back (left) to its head (right) and down along the wearer's left forearm, while in frame 3 the skeleton collapses into a small cluster over the dog's dark face as the dog lifts its head toward the wearer. The map completely fails to detect the magenta hand skeletons for the camera wearer's left hand (holding the dog's neck across all five frames) and right hand (pointing and reaching in from the lower right in frames 1–5), offering no usable spatial information beyond roughly marking the dog's foreground location in the first three frames.
